newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Danish Eurosceptic MEP says court case may paralyse govt.
newsitem.headline: Danish Eurosceptic MEP says court case may paralyse govt.

text.p: A leading Danish Eurosceptic MEP said on Friday that Denmark could not ratify a revised European Union treaty until it has been decided whether the Maastricht treaty is in line with the country's constitution.

A non-partisan group of 11 Danes has filed suit against the government, saying Denmark's ratification of EU treaties could contravene a clause in the constitution limiting how much national sovereignty may be ceded abroad.
"The proceedings before the supreme court can in fact paralyse the Danish government," said Ole Krarup, member of the European Parliament's Europe of Nations Group.

"It would not be able to ratify the Maastricht2 treaty until such a time as we have decided whether or not Maastricht1 is in compliance with the Danish constitution," he told a largely Eurosceptic audience at a conference on the EU's Intergovernmental Conference (IGC).
In August, the Supreme Court surprised Danes and unnerved other EU members by overturning a lower court's refusal to allow the suit, which has been awaiting a hearing since 1993.
Krarup, supporting the suit, said the ruling would have wide-ranging implications.
Every time the EU moves towards further integration countries lose some of their democratic autonomy, he said.
"We are abandoning our right to democratic self-determination in signing this new treaty," he said.
However, last week the Danish citizens' group suffered a setback when court authorities turned down its request to have confidential government documents brought in evidence.
Limiting the scope of the trial, expected to begin in earnest next year, is seen by legal experts as strengthening the government's prospects of a victory.
Defeat could oblige it to renegotiate its EU treaties from scratch or seek to amend the constitution, a tortuous process requiring a general election and a referendum.
Danes have a history of coolness towards the EU.

They rejected Maastricht altogether in a 1992 referendum and approved it the following year only on condition that Denmark stay out of European Monetary Union and joint defence, policing and citizenship arrangements.
